title: KV cache lane isolation and stochastic restoration
body:
Purpose
This is a working draft proposing a complementary approach to our existing slab/pool compaction work: lane isolation combined with stochastic restoration. The goal is to reduce cross-thread fragmentation blowups and reduce tail latency regressions during aggressive reclaim cycles while maintaining high throughput for hot prefixes.

Motivation & problem statement
We observe two recurring failure modes in production: 1) sudden fragmentation storms when large allocations from different tenants/threads interleave leading to long compaction pauses, and 2) eviction oscillation where hot items are evicted and restored repeatedly because background compaction and admission policies are not coordinated with request-level hotness. Existing slab and compacting pools help, but do not fully prevent noisy neighbor effects and suboptimal reclamation timing under mixed workloads.

Key ideas (overview)
- Lane isolation: partition allocation paths into lightweight per-worker lanes (fastpath) and a shared island pool for large/irregular objects. Lanes are not rigid slab sizes; they are logical allocation streams with per-lane metadata (watermarks, occupancy histograms, credit counters).
- Stochastic restoration: perform probabilistic, low-cost restoration of recently-evicted KV entries guided by short-term access sampling. Instead of immediately reloading on first miss, we use a small sampled prefetch/backfill budget to reduce oscillation.
- Gentle reclamation windows: background reclamation runs with randomized jitter windows and incremental thresholds based on fragmentation pressure scores to avoid synchronized global compaction.

Layout and allocation model
- Per-worker lanes: each worker thread has N lanes (N configurable, default 3): hot, warm, cold. Hot lane handles small, recently-accessed prefixes with aggressive lifetime retention and no immediate spill. Warm lane holds less-frequently-used items and is the primary target for opportunistic compaction. Cold lane is the admission sink for large or long-lived entries and is eligible for spill to disk or shared island.
- Island pool: contiguous large-block allocator backed by hugepage-friendly mmap. Island allocations are used for objects that exceed the lane size threshold or when lane occupancy crosses high-water marks.
- Metadata layout: each allocation has a compact header with: lane-id, tag (tenant/model), epoch-id, last-access-sample-bits, approximate-size-class, and a frag-score delta (for quick scoring without full traversal). This keeps per-entry metadata cheap for fast-path lookups.

Eviction and reclamation heuristics
- Local lane eviction: when a lane crosses its soft high watermark, it enrolls a local reclamation job that targets the warm lane first, choosing victims by combined score = alpha * LRU_rank + beta * frag_delta + gamma * tenant_penalty. alpha/beta/gamma are tunables with conservative defaults to bias against deallocating recently hit items and to prefer high-fragmentation contributors.
- Island eviction: island pool uses time-sliced compaction; free lists are coalesced incrementally. A probabilistic sampler inspects allocation adjacency and triggers restitching operations only if coalescing yield is above a threshold.
- Gentle global compaction: instead of immediate full compaction across all lanes, we run staggered windows with per-node seed derived from node-id and recent-uptime to avoid correlated compaction across racks.

Fragmentation scoring and telemetry
- Fragmentation score per lane: maintained as a rolling metric combining occupancy variance, average free-run-length, and per-size-class scarcity. Exposed to Console for route-level alerts.
- Escrow bucket for fragile allocations: small, bounce-prone entries are tracked in a short-lived escrow with a time-to-digest. If an entry exits escrow repeatedly, its placement is migrated to warm lane or island to reduce churn.

Stochastic restoration flow
- On eviction of an entry with recent access history above a threshold, we emit a low-cost sample event (1-5% of such evictions) that seeds a restoration token. Restoration tokens are globally rate-limited per-tenant and consumed by a low-priority backfill worker that prefetches the KV content into the warm lane if access pattern suggests imminent reuse.
- The restoration budget is proportional to the tenant's recent QPS and scaled inversely with current memory pressure to avoid thrashing under low memory headroom.

Thread-aware placement and fairness
- Each lane keeps a tiny token-bank for the worker; when a worker becomes starved (excess soft-evictions), neighboring workers can lend micro-tokens from their warm lane if link-locality and tenant affinity checks pass. This reduces tail pressure for high-burst flows without global reconfiguration.
- Cross-tenant fairness: eviction scores include a tenant-weight multiplier derived from route-level quotas so that a noisy tenant can't evict another tenant's items under normal load.

Operational knobs and safety mechanisms
- Watermarks: per-lane soft/high/critical watermarks that trigger different behaviors (sampling eviction, island spill, emergency fallback to aggressive compaction). Watermarks auto-adjust based on 5-minute occupancy trends.
- Emergency preemption: if tail latency breaches SLOs and memory is high, the system can opt into fast-path spill for cold lane items only while preserving hot lane contents.
- Observability: expose lane-level metrics (occupancy, eviction_rate, frag_score, restore_tokens_consumed) and sample traces for compaction events. Add an alert when restoration rate > eviction rate for > 1 minute (possible oscillation).

Prototype plan and experiments
- Phase 1 (simulator): implement a discrete-event simulator modeling lanes, island pool, and stochastic restoration. Run mixed tenant workloads and compare against baseline slab allocator for P95/P99 latency and total compaction CPU.
- Phase 2 (canary): implement hot/warm/cold lanes in the runtime with opt-in flag, island allocator using existing hugepage pool, and a backfill worker for restoration tokens. Deploy on a limited set of Dedicated clusters behind a feature flag.
- Phase 3 (safety): tune alpha/beta/gamma constants, watermark heuristics, restoration sampling rate, and implement guardrails (max restore tokens per tenant per minute).

Open questions and risks
- Complexity cost: lane metadata and token accounting add bookkeeping; need to quantify steady-state CPU overhead.
- Parameter sensitivity: how sensitive are eviction outcomes to alpha/beta/gamma? We need robust defaults and automated tuning signals.
- Restoration correctness: additional reads for restoration increase I/O; must ensure rate limits and prioritize local memory fetches over remote store on Private deployments.

Next steps
- Assign simulator owner (Diego) and instrumentation owner (Hannah). Draft simulator scenarios and expected baselines by 2025-01-24.
- Early review: pair with SRE to validate emergency preemption interplay with autoscaler and request routing.

Notes to reviewers
- This is a ideation-first draft. Look for correctness of safety nets and whether lane isolation semantics map cleanly onto our worker thread model. Comments inline preferred; heavy edits should be done on the simulator branch PR rather than here.

Summary
Lane isolation + stochastic restoration aims to provide a middle ground between rigid slab allocation and heavy-handed compaction: keep hot paths fast, reduce cross-thread fragmentation storms, and smooth rehydration of recently-evicted items using probabilistic, rate-limited background work. If successful, this should lower P99 tail latency in mixed tenant workloads and cut compaction CPU spikes.
